title: English Vocabulary 2 · Units 27–28
description: Curated countryside vocabulary for natural scenery, farming and rural life; and transport vocabulary for vehicles, boarding, fares, tickets, journeys and services.
sourceNotice: Prepared from user-supplied reference pages. Vocabulary targets follow the source topics; example sentences and teaching notes are newly written. Source exercises, extended passages, and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, labelled natural-environment and vehicle illustrations, transport table, common-mistakes boxes, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for teachable vocabulary and patterns.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for target words and natural phrases, checked with indexed British forms where possible. Connected-speech variations and all accent variants are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.

units.title: Unit 27 — Life in the country
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 27. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe rural scenery using words for landscape, plants, trees and the natural environment.
Talk about growing up in the countryside and about seasonal outdoor activities.
Name common farm features and describe keeping animals and growing crops.
Explain advantages and disadvantages of country life, including access to public transport.
Use key expressions accurately, especially in the countryside, surrounded by nature and apart from.

items.example: She moved to the countryside to enjoy a quieter life.
items.note: The land outside towns and cities, including farms and villages.

items.example: They live in the countryside near a small river.
items.note: Say in the countryside; do not use in the nature.

items.example: He prefers living in the country to living in the city.
items.note: In this sense, the country means rural areas; compare countryside.

items.example: My cousins grew up on a farm.
items.note: Past tense: grew up. Used for the place or circumstances of childhood.

items.example: We enjoy nature on our walks outside the village.
items.note: The natural world: plants, animals and landscape.

items.example: The little house is surrounded by nature.
items.note: Surrounded by means having something on all sides; avoid in the nature.

items.example: We had lunch on the river bank.
items.note: The land beside a river; bank has other meanings in different contexts.

items.example: A narrow river runs through the valley.
items.note: A natural flow of water across the land.

items.example: We walked through the woods after lunch.
items.note: An area with many trees; normally plural in this sense.

items.example: We often pick fruit in the autumn.
items.note: Pick means take fruit or flowers from the plant, rather than select one from a shop.

items.example: It is important to know which mushrooms are safe before you pick them.
items.note: Collect mushrooms growing outdoors; distinct from buying them.

items.example: There are plenty of blackberries near the path.
items.note: Small dark berries that grow on bushes.

items.example: Autumn is her favourite season.
items.note: The year has four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter.

items.example: The trees become green again in spring.
items.note: The season after winter and before summer.

items.example: The days are longer in summer.
items.note: The warmest season in many places.

items.example: The leaves change colour in autumn.
items.note: British English: autumn; also called fall in American English.

items.example: It often freezes here in winter.
items.note: The season after autumn and before spring.

items.example: The scenery around the lake is beautiful.
items.note: The appearance of natural surroundings; usually uncountable.

items.pt: espaços abertos; áreas amplas sem construções
items.example: Children have plenty of open spaces to play in.
items.note: Large areas of land without many buildings.

items.example: We went for a walk to get some fresh air.
items.note: Air that feels clean, especially away from pollution.

items.example: There is an old tree at the end of the garden.
items.note: A large plant with a woody trunk and branches.

items.example: A bird was sitting on one of the branches.
items.note: A part of a tree growing out of its trunk; plural branches.

items.example: A yellow leaf fell from the tree.
items.note: The flat green part of a plant; irregular plural leaves.

items.example: Wet leaves covered the footpath.
items.note: The irregular plural of leaf.

items.example: The roots of the tree spread under the ground.
items.note: The parts of a plant that grow underground.

items.example: Many wild plants grow beside the path.
items.note: Living things that grow in soil or water, including flowers and shrubs.

items.example: The grass was still wet in the morning.
items.note: The short green plants covering lawns and fields; usually uncountable.

items.example: The ground was muddy after the rain.
items.note: The earth under your feet outdoors; contrasts with a floor inside.

items.example: They run a farm with sheep and vegetables.
items.note: Land and buildings used to grow crops or keep animals.

items.example: My aunt owns a small farm.
items.note: Have something that legally belongs to you; different from manage.

items.example: The family keeps chickens and goats.
items.note: Keep animals means own and look after them.

items.example: The farmers grow crops such as wheat and potatoes.
items.note: Grow crops for food or other uses; different from keeping animals.

items.example: The drought damaged the crops.
items.note: Plants grown by farmers, often for food or sale.

items.example: Farming can involve long working days.
items.note: The work of producing crops and raising animals.

items.pt: estar acordado e fora da cama cedo
items.example: Farmers often have to be up early.
items.note: Be up means be out of bed; different from get up, the action of leaving bed.

items.example: We sat outside and watched the sunset.
items.note: The time when the sun goes down in the evening.

items.example: The farmhouse is at the top of a hill.
items.note: Land that rises above the surrounding area, usually smaller than a mountain.

items.example: A stream flows through the valley.
items.note: A low area of land between hills or mountains.

items.example: The sheep were grazing in a large field.
items.note: An area of land used for farming or animals.

items.pt: casa de fazenda; sede da fazenda
items.example: They invited us into the old farmhouse.
items.note: The main house on a farm.

items.example: There is a wooden fence around the field.
items.note: A structure marking a boundary or keeping animals inside.

items.example: Please close the gate after entering the field.
items.note: A movable barrier in a fence or wall.

items.example: A tractor was working in the next field.
items.note: A powerful vehicle used on farms.

items.pt: trilha para pedestres; caminho a pé
items.example: The footpath crosses the field and enters the woods.
items.note: A path intended for people walking, rather than cars.

items.pt: caminhar ao lado de; acompanhar lateralmente
items.example: We walked alongside the fence until we reached a gate.
items.note: Alongside means next to and in the same direction.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: The village has a shop and a small school.
items.note: A settlement smaller than a town.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: There is little to do apart from walking and cycling.
items.note: Used to introduce an exception or an additional item.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: The nearest town is ten miles away.
items.note: Nearest is the superlative of near.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: The station is several miles away.
items.note: An expression showing distance from a place; a mile is a distance unit.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: Public transport is limited in this village.
items.note: Buses, trains and similar services used by the public.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: The bus service here is hopeless.
items.note: Informal, strong negative judgement: extremely bad or ineffective.

items.pt: não há muita coisa para fazer
items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: There is not much to do here after dark.
items.note: A useful expression for a place with few activities.

items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: There are not many shops in the village.
items.note: Natural alternative to you do not get many shops in this area.

items.pt: bem longe; a uma longa distância
items.section: C · The disadvantages of country life
items.example: The nearest hospital is a long way away.
items.note: Describes a considerable distance from the place mentioned.

units.title: Unit 28 — Transport
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 28. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify common road vehicles, types of transport and people who operate them.
Use the appropriate verbs and prepositions for travelling by bus, train, plane, taxi and bicycle.
Distinguish get on/off for buses and trains from get in/out of for cars and taxis.
Talk about fares, tickets, transport facilities, regular services and delays.
Use journey rather than travel for a particular trip, and discuss reliability and complaints.

items.example: Only emergency vehicles may use this road.
items.note: A general word for means of road transport.

items.example: The bus stops outside the library.
items.note: A large vehicle carrying passengers along a regular route.

items.example: We travelled to the seaside by coach.
items.note: In British English, a coach usually takes passengers on longer journeys; compare bus.

items.example: The shop uses a van to deliver orders.
items.note: A road vehicle used to transport goods or a small group of people.

items.example: My bicycle has a basket on the front.
items.note: A two-wheeled vehicle that you ride by pedalling; short form: bike.

items.example: She rides her bike to school.
items.note: Often means bicycle; can sometimes refer to a motorbike.

items.example: He wears a helmet whenever he rides his motorbike.
items.note: A two-wheeled road vehicle with an engine; say ride a motorbike.

items.example: A lorry was unloading food at the market.
items.note: British English; truck is the common American English equivalent.

items.example: The truck carried furniture to the new house.
items.note: Often the American English equivalent of British lorry.

items.example: The train arrives at seven fifteen.
items.note: Rail transport; you get on or off a train.

items.example: Our plane was delayed by heavy fog.
items.note: A vehicle used for air travel.

items.example: We took a taxi from the airport.
items.note: A car you pay to take you somewhere; you get in or out of it.

items.example: The bus driver waited while we bought tickets.
items.note: The person who drives a bus.

items.example: The train driver stopped at the red signal.
items.note: The person who operates a train.

items.example: The pilot announced that we would land soon.
items.note: The person who flies an aircraft.

items.example: The taxi driver knew a faster route.
items.note: The person who drives a taxi.

items.example: Several cyclists were waiting at the lights.
items.note: Someone riding a bicycle.

items.example: I cycle to work when the weather is good.
items.note: Verb: travel by bicycle.

items.example: The fare to the airport was quite expensive.
items.note: The price paid for a trip by bus, train or taxi; not a fee for all services.

items.pt: tarifa de ônibus; preço da passagem
items.example: The bus fare went up last month.
items.note: The cost of one or more journeys by bus.

items.pt: tarifa ferroviária; preço da passagem de trem
items.example: Train fares are cheaper if you book early.
items.note: The price of travel by train.

items.pt: tarifa aérea; preço de passagem de avião
items.example: Airfares often rise during the summer holidays.
items.note: The price of an air journey; often used in the plural airfares.

items.pt: as tarifas aumentam; as passagens ficam mais caras
items.example: Fares usually go up at the start of the year.
items.note: Go up means increase in price; contrast go down.

items.example: We must leave now to catch the last bus.
items.note: Catch a bus means board it in time, often at a stop.

items.pt: pegar o ônibus; ir de ônibus
items.example: I usually get the bus to university.
items.note: British English: take or catch the bus are also natural.

items.example: We decided to get the train to the city centre.
items.note: British English alternative to take the train.

items.example: They go by bus because parking is difficult.
items.note: Use by + transport without a/an/the when describing the means.

items.example: We prefer to go by train on long trips.
items.note: Use by train, not by the train, when naming the general means.

items.example: We are going to fly to Edinburgh.
items.note: Travel by plane, or operate an aircraft; past tense: flew.

items.example: Let us take a taxi to the station.
items.note: A common expression for hiring and travelling in a taxi.

items.example: My son is learning to ride a bike.
items.note: Use ride, not drive, when travelling on a bicycle.

items.example: She knows how to ride a motorbike.
items.note: Use ride a motorbike, not drive a motorbike.

items.example: We got on a bus near the museum.
items.note: Use get on with buses, trains, planes and bicycles.

items.example: Get off the bus at the next stop.
items.note: Use get off with buses, trains, planes and bicycles.

items.example: We got on the train at platform four.
items.note: Use get on a train, not get in a train, for normal boarding.

items.example: We got off the train at the last station.
items.note: Use get off for leaving trains, buses and planes.

items.example: The children got in the car and put on their seat belts.
items.note: Use get in a car or taxi, not get on a car.

items.example: I got out of the taxi outside the hotel.
items.note: Use get out of a car or taxi, not get off a taxi.

items.example: The bus stop is opposite the pharmacy.
items.note: A place where buses stop to pick up passengers.

items.example: The coach leaves from the bus station.
items.note: A place where many buses or coaches begin or end journeys.

items.example: Meet me outside the train station.
items.note: A place where people board and leave trains.

items.example: The train to Oxford leaves from platform six.
items.note: The raised area at a station beside the train; your departure may be from platform six.

items.example: We arrived at the airport two hours early.
items.note: The place where planes take off, land and passengers check in.

items.example: There is a taxi rank outside the station.
items.note: British English for a designated place where taxis wait for customers.

items.example: The journey from the station took about an hour.
items.note: A particular trip from one place to another; do not use a travel in this sense.

items.pt: viagem em geral; ato de viajar
items.example: Travel is often more relaxing by train.
items.note: Often an uncountable noun for travelling in general; use a journey for one particular trip.

items.example: Our flight landed ten minutes early.
items.note: An air journey by plane; plural flights.

items.pt: parada de ônibus; ponto na rota
items.example: It is only three stops from here.
items.note: A stop is one of the places where a bus halts along its route.

items.example: Public transport is better in the city centre.
items.note: Public buses, trains and similar services; British English transport is normally uncountable.

items.example: The bus stop is convenient because it is near our house.
items.note: Easy or practical to use; the opposite here is inconvenient.

items.pt: o ponto de ônibus mais próximo
items.example: The nearest bus stop is ten minutes away on foot.
items.note: The nearest identifies the closest location; do not confuse nearest with next.

items.example: The nearest station is half a mile away.
items.note: A distance expression using half a mile and away.

items.example: We had to wait in a queue to buy tickets.
items.note: British English queue means a line of waiting people.

items.example: Two buses came along after twenty minutes.
items.note: A vehicle or person arrives or passes by; past tense came along.

items.example: Passengers often complain about delayed trains.
items.note: Complain about + noun or -ing form; related noun: complaint.

items.example: She made a complaint about the service.
items.note: Noun from complain; common phrase: make a complaint.

items.pt: serviço de ônibus; operação de linhas de ônibus
items.example: The bus service has improved this year.
items.note: A regular service provided by buses on a route.

items.pt: logo ali na esquina; muito perto
items.example: There is a bus stop just round the corner.
items.note: British English expression meaning very nearby, often around the next corner.

items.pt: circular; passar a cada dez minutos
items.example: The buses run every ten minutes during the day.
items.note: Run can mean operate according to a timetable; not physically run on foot.

items.pt: confiável; pontual; que funciona como esperado
items.example: Trains on this line are usually reliable.
items.note: A service you can depend on; often used to discuss public transport.

items.example: I bought a return ticket to Bristol.
items.note: British English: a ticket covering travel there and back; often shortened to a return.

items.example: A single ticket costs less than a return.
items.note: A ticket for one journey in one direction; contrasts with return ticket.

items.pt: passe mensal; passe por período; bilhete de temporada
items.example: She has a season ticket for her daily train commute.
items.note: A ticket valid for many journeys during a specified period.

items.pt: perder o trem; não conseguir embarcar
items.example: If we miss the train, we will be late for the meeting.
items.note: Miss means fail to catch the transport in time; not lose it as a possession.

items.example: We decided to make a complaint about the late bus.
items.note: Use make a complaint, not do a complaint.

items.example: The train will depart from platform two.
items.note: A formal transport verb; depart from + a place or platform.
